statement: Five friends sit in a row of 5 seats for a photo. Mia insists on sitting at one of the two ends of the row. In how many different orders can the five friends sit?

choices.misconception: I only let Mia sit at the left end and forgot she could sit at the right end too.
I counted all the orders of the five friends and ignored Mia's wish.
I worked out the orders where Mia is not at an end, 120 - 48, instead of the ones where she is.
I placed Mia in 2 ways and then added the choices for the other seats, 4 + 3 + 2 + 1 = 10, instead of multiplying them.

hints: Mia has a choice of seats. Once she is seated, the other four friends fill the remaining four seats in any order. Use the multiplication principle.
Mia has 2 choices. The other four can be arranged in $4 \times 3 \times 2 \times 1 = 24$ ways.

solutions.reliable: Mia can take the left end or the right end: 2 ways. Then the other four friends fill the 4 remaining seats: 4 choices for the first free seat, 3 for the next, then 2, then 1, which is 24 ways. So there are $2 \times 24 = 48$ orders. The transferable idea: place the restricted person first, then arrange everyone else.
solutions.elegant: Over all 120 orders, Mia is in each of the 5 seats equally often, so 2 out of every 5 orders put her at an end: $120 \times 2 \div 5 = 48$.

whyOnTest: Tests arrangements with one restriction: place the restricted person first, then multiply by the arrangements of the rest.
author: Devansh Sanghavi
